places.name: Antigua Guatemala

visits.text: Antigua was founded in 1543 as Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala — Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Cortés's former companion, served as its governor for years. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the city spreads across the Panchoy Valley, framed by three volcanoes: Agua (3,760 m, dormant), Fuego (3,763 m, active), and Acatenango (3,976 m). Start at the Parque Central: surrounding it you'll find the Catedral de Santiago (only its grand facade remains after the 1773 earthquakes), the Palace of the Captains General, and the City Hall. Take a moment to sit on a bench and soak it in — this is when the locals come together.

The Arco de Santa Catalina is the city's most iconic landmark: this saffron-yellow arch was built in 1694 to let cloistered nuns from the convent cross the street unseen. The clock crowning it is a Lamy & Lacroix made in France, added in the 1830s — it's still wound by hand every three days. Get there before 8 AM to avoid the tour groups and catch Volcán Agua framed in the background. From Calle del Arco, you also get a clear line of sight to La Merced church.

Iglesia La Merced, instantly recognisable by its bright yellow and white facade in the Spanish baroque style, is one of the best-preserved churches in Antigua. Its cloister houses a fountain 27 metres in diameter — the largest in Central America. Climb to the roof for a view over the fountain and the city's tiled rooftops.

The Convento de Las Capuchinas, founded in 1736, is one of the best-preserved ruined convents in the city. Its circular galleries of cells arranged around a central tower are unique in colonial American architecture. Light filters through the collapsed vaults — the atmosphere is striking. Allow 45 minutes.

Head up to Cerro de la Cruz in the late afternoon: this viewpoint north of the city offers the finest panorama of Antigua and all three volcanoes. The climb from the centre takes about 20 minutes on foot. Time it for golden hour — the volcanoes take on an orange glow that contrasts beautifully with the city's red-tiled roofs.

Hobbitenango is an ecological park perched in the hills above Antigua, designed as a nod to the world of Tolkien — round houses, gentle sloping paths through the pines, and unobstructed views over all three volcanoes and the valley below. It's mainly a good excuse to take a breath and enjoy the scenery without any effort. Allow 1 hour on site.

Back from Pacaya in the late afternoon, make a final detour to Convento Santo Domingo — the largest convent in Antigua, whose construction dates back to the Dominicans who arrived in Guatemala in 1538. Destroyed by the 1773 earthquake, its ruins now house a museum and interior gardens. The collapsed nave is one of the most photographed spots in the city: the open ceiling lets light pour in as if it were an open-air cathedral. Paid entry; allow 40 minutes.

Chichicastenango (or 'Chichi') sits at 1,965 metres in the Quiché highlands, a 1h30 drive from Panajachel. Its market, one of the largest in Central America, has been held on Thursdays and Sundays for centuries — traders from across the region converge at dawn to sell textiles, pottery, dance masks, medicinal plants, copal, and corn. Arrive at opening (around 6 AM) to watch the stalls go up before the tour-bus wave hits around 9:30.

The Iglesia de Santo Tomás, built around 1545 on the platform of a Maya temple, is the most striking example of religious syncretism in Guatemala. Its 18 steps represent the 18 months of the Maya calendar — K'iche' shamans burn copal incense and swing their censers on them throughout the day. Inside, the floor is strewn with flower petals and candles arranged in precise patterns, while worshippers murmur prayers in the Quiché language. Photography inside is strictly forbidden. Enter through the side door and stay silent.

The cemetery of Chichicastenango is one of the country's most striking surprises: its mausoleums and headstones are painted turquoise (for mothers), white (for fathers), and yellow (for grandparents), creating an explosion of colour on the hillside. Maya and Catholic rituals coexist here on a daily basis. Not to be missed if you have any appreciation for popular funerary art.

Pascual Abaj (Sacrifice Stone) is a Maya shrine on a hilltop 20 minutes' walk south of town. The path leads through the cemetery. At the top, a black stone idol represents Huyup Tak'ah, the Earth God — K'iche' shamans still perform daily ceremonies here with offerings, candles, and incense. Access is open but respectful behaviour is expected.

activities.text: Wander the cobblestoned alleys between two ruined convents: Santa Clara (founded in 1700 — its collapsed arches frame the sky like perfect oculi) and Santo Domingo (destroyed in the 1773 earthquake, its interior gardens partly repurposed). Both sites can be covered in about an hour and a half total.

Local operators offer Guatemalan cooking classes or food tours through the streets of Antigua — a great way to learn the basics of the local cuisine (pepián, kak'ik, hand-pressed tortillas) alongside locals. Failing that, the Mercado Municipal, steps from the centre, is ideal for a no-frills lunch.

The hike up Pacaya is the most accessible volcanic excursion in Guatemala. The volcano stands at 2,552 metres and remains one of the country's three active volcanoes alongside Fuego and Santiaguito. From the entrance of the Parque Nacional Volcán Pacaya (at San Francisco de Sales, 1 hour from Antigua), the trail loops 5.6 km with 453 metres of elevation gain — allow 2h30 to 3h round trip. The pine forest gradually gives way to a black, lunar landscape of solidified lava. At the summit, fissures release sulphurous heat — guides will offer to roast marshmallows on sticks. The views from the top take in Agua, Fuego, and Acatenango. Leave early in the morning (before 11 AM the cone is often shrouded in cloud). A guide is mandatory on site.

Back in Antigua in the evening, a night-time stroll through the lamp-lit cobblestone streets reveals a different city entirely: the coloured facades take on coppery tones under the lantern light. A terrace at one of the cafés around the Parque Central is perfect for a last cold beer before heading to the lake the next day.

Plunge into the market aisles in search of the best finds: huipiles (embroidered blouses) and ceremonial dance masks are Chichicastenango's specialities. Vendors on the north side of the square sell more authentic handcrafted goods; the tourist-oriented stalls cluster near the south entrance. Take your time: bargaining is expected, and artisans appreciate visitors who stop to look properly.
Shuttle back to Antigua (about 3 hours by road via Chimaltenango). Overnight in Antigua to ease the airport transfer the following morning.

places.name: Arroyo Pucte

visits.text: The Arroyo Pucté jetty is the only practical access point to the Cráter Azul, a few kilometres down a dirt track past Los Josefinos. Free parking, a couple of ice-cream sellers, nothing else. It's also the starting point for the other springs of the El Pucté reserve, less visited than the crater itself.

activities.text: You'll only reach the site by lancha, from the Arroyo Pucté jetty or from Sayaxché depending on the route chosen. The crossing passes through river channels and flooded forest, with turtles and waterbirds along the way. Book the boat in advance: on site, prices harden noticeably.

visits.text: Cerro Chino is the park's best viewpoint, and it is not the summit: this secondary cone overlooks the Meseta's black lava flows without requiring the full ascent. The contrast is stark between the pine forest below and the basalt field above. Closed shoes are compulsory, as the volcanic rock cuts thin soles.

activities.text: Guides call the smoking fissures 'los hornitos', the little ovens. Some visitors toast marshmallows there on a skewer, a gesture that has become an accepted ritual, and a pizza oven runs on the heat of the ground near the visitor post. Kitsch, but feeling the warm ground underfoot stays memorable.

places.name: Chiantla

visits.text: The Parroquia Nuestra Señora de Candelaria de Chiantla houses a sixteenth-century Virgin whose mantle is forged in silver, a gift from Spaniards enriched by the nearby silver mines in the seventeenth century. Hence its local nickname, the Virgen de Plata. The patronal feast on 2 February draws thousands of pilgrims; the rest of the year, the church is almost empty.

If the Cuchumatanes road is clear, the Mirador Juan Diéguez Olaverri, above Chiantla, opens out onto the whole plateau. The Huehuetenango-born poet has an engraved stele there. You climb quickly above 3,000 metres: the wind is bitterly cold even in bright sunshine, so keep a fleece in the car.

activities.text: Thin air, close-cropped grass, sheep among the rocks: the Cuchumatanes altiplano is like nowhere else in Guatemala. The road climbs in tight switchbacks from Chiantla and the landscape shifts within twenty minutes. Stop at the marked viewpoints rather than on the verge, as visibility is short on the bends.

map_keywords: Parroquia Nuestra Senora de Candelaria Chiantla

visits.text: Go to Chichicastenango on Sunday, not Thursday—the market is even denser, and vendors come from across the Altiplano. It's one of Central America's largest indigenous markets, though don't claim it's the oldest or largest without nuance: local sources make it a point of national pride—that's enough. Guard your bag and bargain with a cool head.

Built in 1540, Santo Tomás church rises on the foundations of an ancient Maya temple. The eighteen steps leading to its entrance are still considered sacred by the K'iche', and shamans burn incense and copal there daily. This is where the Popol Vuh manuscript, sacred Maya book, was rediscovered in the 18th century. Don't photograph inside, and cover shoulders and knees.

Chichicastenango's cemetery explodes with color: tombstones painted yellow, turquoise, magenta, Maya and Catholic rituals intertwined. Five minutes on foot from the market, the visit is discreet and respectful, especially on days of family offerings.

activities.text: Climb Santo Tomás's steps to see the market from above—the labyrinthine sprawl of stalls becomes legible from up here. The Calvario chapel on the opposite side of the plaza offers the same kind of viewpoint but with fewer crowds.

If you really want to bargain, divide the announced price by two and work your way up slowly. Embroidered huipiles and traditional dance masks are the most typical purchases. Avoid religious feast days like December 7 (Quema del Diablo), when the town closes for business.

visits.text: Head back to Río Dulce by lancha (1h15), then drive to Cobán via the northern shore of Lake Izabal — expect 4 to 5 hours of travel in total. The transition is striking: you leave the Caribbean heat behind and climb into the misty mountains of Alta Verapaz, above 1,300 metres. Founded in 1543 by Dominican friars, Cobán was dubbed 'the city among the clouds' by the Q'eqchi' people. In the 19th century, a wave of German settlers arrived to develop the coffee plantations — their influence is still visible in the architecture.

The Vivero Verapaz, a 30-minute walk from the centre, is a former coffee estate converted into an orchid conservatory. It houses around 650 different species. The best time to visit is between November and January, when the grounds erupt in a spectacular carpet of colour during peak blooming season. Outside this window, it's still a remarkable botanical garden.

The Museo El Príncipe Maya, tucked away on the main square, holds a private collection of ceramics, jewellery, and pre-Columbian artefacts from the Q'eqchi' region. It's a useful introduction before heading to Semuc Champey — the site was considered sacred by the Maya, and the museum provides valuable context.

Full day at Semuc Champey, 65 km from Cobán — allow 1h30 of driving, the last 20 kilometres on a bumpy dirt track. Join a shuttle from your accommodation or hire a pick-up. Semuc Champey means 'where the water hides in the stone' in Q'eqchi': the Cahabón River vanishes beneath a 300-metre natural limestone bridge, and above it a series of cascading pools has formed, their colour shifting from azure to emerald depending on the light. Leave by 8 AM — organised tour groups typically don't arrive until after 1 PM.

Hike up to the Semuc Champey viewpoint: allow 30 to 45 minutes of steep climbing through the jungle from the site entrance. The bird's-eye view over the entire chain of cascading pools, framed by tropical forest, is Guatemala's most iconic photograph. The trail is tough when it's wet — proper walking shoes beat sandals every time. Head straight down to the pools for a swim afterwards.

Explore the Kamba (Kanba) Caves, adjacent to the pools. The tour is done by candlelight, wading through waist-deep water in places, squeezing through narrow passages, and sliding down natural rock chutes. A local guide is essential — they'll adapt to your level. Not for the claustrophobic, but for everyone else, it's an unforgettable experience.

The Biotopo del Quetzal, an hour south of Cobán on the road to Guatemala City, is one of the few reserves where you can still spot a quetzal in the wild — this iridescent green bird with a long red tail was sacred to the Maya. The site offers two trails through the cloud forest (2 km and 4 km). Arrive early, before 9 AM, to maximise your chances. Even without a quetzal sighting, the moss-draped, epiphyte-laden forest is worth the trip on its own.

Orquigonia is a botanical garden dedicated to orchid conservation, and can be visited in about an hour and a half with a guide. The trail runs roughly 1 km through grounds planted with hundreds of orchid species and epiphytes. The guides are excellent educators — they'll teach you how to tell species apart and lend you a magnifying glass. The view from the garden's mirador over the valley is an added bonus.

Las Victorias National Park sits right within the city of Cobán, northwest of the centre — a pocket of primary forest woven into the urban fabric, crisscrossed by marked trails. You can picnic, watch birds, and stroll away from the bustle. Entry is free.

activities.text: Visit Finca Santa Margarita to learn where Cobán's coffee comes from — widely regarded as some of Guatemala's finest. The guided tour of the plantation walks you through the entire process, from picking to roasting. The cool, humid climate of Alta Verapaz, with its persistent local drizzle known as chipi-chipi, creates ideal conditions for the slow maturation of the beans.

Try kak'ik at a local restaurant in the town centre. This spicy turkey stew, served with tamalitos (corn dough wrapped in dried banana leaves), is a traditional Q'eqchi' dish recognised as intangible cultural heritage. It's Cobán's quintessential speciality — don't leave without trying it at least once.

Swim in the natural pools at Semuc Champey. The water is refreshing — some shallow pools let you stretch out on the limestone rocks, while others reach two to three metres deep. Head down to the lower pools, which see far fewer visitors: you'll often have the small cascades trickling over the stone all to yourself.

Tubing on the Cahabón River on the way back from Semuc Champey: you float downstream on an inner tube through a stretch of fast-moving rapids covering several hundred metres. Local operators run this activity from the village of Lanquín, 11 km from the site. Bring a change of clothes.

Browse Cobán's artisan market in the morning: Q'eqchi' textiles, silver jewellery, and cardamom-based products (the region's top export crop) are sold directly by the producers. Cobán is also one of the world's cardamom capitals — you'll catch its scent on every street corner.

In the late afternoon, settle into a café on the main square and savour some locally grown Alta Verapaz coffee. The light mist — the famous chipi-chipi — that often wraps around Cobán in the evening gives the town a soft, melancholic atmosphere unlike anywhere else. A fine excuse to linger over a hot cup.

visits.text: Water so clear navy blue that you can see the bottom several metres down: the Cráter Azul is a spring of the Río La Pasión, within the El Pucté wildlife refuge. Water lilies, submerged trunks and ochre and green vegetation form a kind of garden beneath the surface. Five to seven metres at the centre, almost nothing at the edges.

activities.text: Mask and snorkel change everything here, far more than swimming alone. The visibility lets you follow shoals of fish above the submerged vegetation. Watch out for the current if you move away from the entry point: it pushes harder than it appears on the way back.

places.name: Flores

visits.text: The island of Flores, former capital of the last independent Mayan state, held out against the conquistadors until 1697 — a full 150 years after the fall of the rest of the empire. Landing at Santa Elena airport (FRS), you cross the causeway connecting the mainland to the island and find yourself in a maze of cobbled lanes and colorful facades perched on the shores of Lake Petén Itzá. Stroll along the malecón, the waterfront promenade that circles the island, in the late afternoon — the light on the lake is remarkable at that hour.

The Parque Central de Flores is the heart of the island, overlooked by the white cathedral Nuestra Señora de los Remedios. It was on this very spot that the Spanish built their town in 1697 using stones from the main Mayan temple they had just destroyed. Take the time to sit in the square and observe local life, very different from that of Santa Elena, the more working-class mainland district.

From the island's dock, hop on a lancha (a 5- to 10-minute crossing) to the village of San Miguel on the north shore of the lake. The Mirador del Rey Canek, with its brightly painted viewing platform, offers the best panoramic view of Flores island and Lake Petén Itzá. From up here, you begin to understand why the Itzá people chose this island setting for their capital — a natural defensive position on the water.

Tikal, about 65 km from Flores and a 1-hour-15-minute drive away, is worth getting up early for—ideally before 6 am to be among the first visitors. The city, inhabited from 600 BC until AD 900, was home to one of the most powerful Maya kingdoms in Central America. Its monumental center covers more than 16 km², with nearly 3,000 recorded structures. On the Gran Plaza, Temple I (Temple of the Great Jaguar, 47 m high) contains the tomb of King Jasaw Chan K'awiil and faces Temple II (Temple of the Masks, 38 m), built in memory of his wife. Arrive early and wait for the howler monkeys to begin their morning chorus in the treetops—the sound is truly impressive.

Temple IV reaches a height of 65 m. From its platform at the top, the summits of the other pyramids rise above the canopy like islands in a sea of green—this is exactly the scenery that inspired the scene on the planet Yavin in Star Wars (Episode IV, 1977). In 2021, LiDAR technology revealed that an entire neighborhood buried beneath the jungle exactly reproduces the architecture of Teotihuacan (Mexico), more than 900 km away—evidence of a far more cosmopolitan city than previously thought.

The Mundo Perdido (Lost World) complex, in the southwestern part of the site, was named by archaeologists after Arthur Conan Doyle's novel because the surrounding jungle reminded them so strongly of its setting. Its main pyramid (30 m) is the oldest structure at Tikal, adorned with stucco masks depicting the sun god. From its summit, you can take in Temples I, II, III and IV in a single view—one of the best panoramas on the site.

In the afternoon, head to Yaxhá, about 73 km from Flores and a 1-hour-30-minute drive away. Yaxhá means “blue-green water” in Maya—a name the city has borne since the Classic period without ever changing it. With around 500 identified structures (including 9 pyramid temples, 2 ball courts and 40 carved stelae), it is the third-largest archaeological site in Guatemala.

The North Acropolis of Yaxhá comprises three nearly intact pyramids, two of which are accessible. From their summits, the unobstructed view over the canopy and the two lagoons is breathtaking. These are the best-preserved structures on the site, remaining in an almost original state—it is fascinating to see what these buildings looked like before any restoration.

Temple 216, the highest point at Yaxhá (over 30 m high), is the must-visit spot for sunset. Archaeologists found handprints painted in red during excavations—hence its nickname, the Temple of the Red Hands. Head up in the late afternoon: from the platform, you can see the jungle stretching as far as the eye can see, the two lagoons flanking the city and, on a clear day, the pyramids of Tikal rising above the forest on the horizon. There are far fewer people than at Tikal to experience this moment.

activities.text: Flight from Guatemala City (GUA) to Flores/Santa Elena (FRS): about 40 minutes; book in advance with local airlines. It's by far the most practical option—the journey by road from the capital takes more than 8 to 10 hours. Collect your bags at Mundo Maya International Airport in Santa Elena and catch a tuk-tuk to the island (a few minutes from the airport to the causeway).

Dinner from the street food stands that set up along the lakefront in the evening, near the bridge at the entrance to Flores. Empanadas, Guatemalan tacos, burritos — everything is eaten standing up, facing the lake as night falls. The vibe is thoroughly local and much cheaper than the touristy terraces on the island itself.

Wildlife spotting in Tikal National Park: howler and spider monkeys in the trees, toucans, macaws, coatis, and for the lucky few, an ocelot or puma on the trails. Bring binoculars — the park harbors an exceptional density of species. Local guides are excellent at spotting elusive animals, and hiring one for the day is well worth it.

Return to Flores in the evening. Organized shuttles from Flores cover both Tikal and Yaxhá in a single day—the most practical way to visit both sites without a car. Fair warning: it's a packed day (4 to 5 hours at Tikal in the morning, 1 hour 30 minutes on the road, 2 to 3 hours at Yaxhá in the afternoon). If the pace feels too intense, save Yaxhá for a separate half-day and stay an extra night in Flores. Both parks charge admission; prices are available on site.

places.name: Guatemala City

visits.text: Arrival at La Aurora International Airport and your first encounter with the capital. Guatemala City is the largest metropolis in Central America — don't let its reputation put you off. Zona 1, the historic center, is well worth half a day. Everything revolves around the Plaza de la Constitución, where the Palacio Nacional de la Cultura showcases early 20th-century official architecture. Allow about 45 minutes to explore its halls.

The Museo Popol Vuh, housed on the campus of Universidad Francisco Marroquín, holds one of the continent's largest collections of Maya art. Inside you'll find pre-Hispanic ceramics, funerary masks, and a reproduction of the Popol Vuh — the Maya creation text discovered in Chichicastenango in the 18th century. Set aside at least 90 minutes to take it all in without rushing.

Drive back from Antigua to Guatemala City (45 min). Use this transition day to visit what you missed on Day 1: the Museo Nacional de Arqueología y Etnología in Zona 13, which brings together Maya stelae, ceramics, and jade funerary masks. It's solid context-setting before heading into the eastern part of the country.

Last long day on the road: Flores to Guatemala City, roughly 8 hours via the CA-13 and then the CA-9. Leave early. If you arrive by mid-afternoon, the Museo Nacional de Arqueología y Etnología in Zona 13 is the fitting finale for an itinerary steeped in the Maya world — stelae, ceramics, jade funerary masks, and scale models of Tikal.

Final morning in Guatemala City. The Mercado Central in Zona 1, just behind the cathedral, is the perfect place to pick up local crafts: embroidered textiles, ceramics, jade items, and Alta Verapaz coffee sold in whole beans or ground on the spot.

activities.text: Dive into the pedestrian 6th Avenue in Zona 1 — this is where Guatemala City shows its true colors: street vendors, open-air markets, locals heading home from work. The Mercado Central, just behind the cathedral, is the perfect spot to try your first local meal (chicken pepián, tamales) and soak up everyday life without a tourist filter.

In the evening, head to Paseo de la Reforma in Zona 10 for a drink on a terrace. This upscale neighborhood is a world apart from the historic center — skyscrapers, contemporary art galleries, restaurants. It's a good place to catch your breath before the three weeks ahead.
Get your gear ready for the east — stock up on cash, as ATMs become scarce past Río Dulce. Have dinner in the Zona Viva for one last urban evening before several days immersed in nature.

Evening in the Zona Viva (Zona 10): this is the liveliest neighborhood in the capital, packed with restaurants and cafés open late. After three weeks in villages and jungle, it's a welcome transition before departure.

Transfer to La Aurora International Airport (GUA), located in Zona 13, 15 to 30 minutes from the Zona Viva depending on traffic. Rush-hour traffic in Guatemala City can be brutal — allow at least 2 hours before your flight.

visits.text: Restored in the 1940s, Zaculeu looks like no other Maya site in the country: pyramids with smoothed-over surfaces, almost like new. The approach is divisive, but it makes the layout of the plazas and ball court immediately easy to read. Capital of the Mam kingdom, the city fell in 1525 after a siege of several months, its defenders starved. The site is 3.7 km from the town centre.

activities.text: The Unicornio Azul is a remote finca in the aldea of Chancol, around 25km from Huehuetenango, a 1-hour-15-minute drive, and at nearly 3,000 metres of altitude. Eight rooms, dinner taken together, a fireplace. The generator switches off at night: a head torch is useful, and a hot water bottle is provided.

The horse ride at the Unicornio Azul is the real reason for this stage, more than Huehuetenango itself. About a dozen horses, open trails across the plateau, and an hour included in the room rate for two people. Let them know when booking if you have never ridden before.

days_plan.itin_title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean

visits.text: San Juan La Laguna is worth it, San Pedro is not. Lake Atitlán, a caldera formed 84,000 years ago and surrounded by three volcanoes (San Pedro, Tolimán, Atitlán), shelters eleven villages with very different personalities. San Juan: street art, Tz'utujil textile cooperatives, coffee. Santiago: traditional market, veneration of Maximón. San Pedro: backpackers in binge-drinking mode.

activities.text: Take the lancha early in the morning from Panajachel—the lake is mirror-smooth and the light beats any filter. About 25 quetzales per trip to San Juan or Santiago; ask for the last return time before you leave. Three villages in a day is doable. Four and you'll miss your siesta.

places.name: Lanquin

visits.text: The Flores-to-Lanquín journey is one of the most spectacular crossings in Guatemala: you leave the lowland forest of Petén and enter the misty mountains of Alta Verapaz. Count on roughly 7 to 8 hours on the road, often in a shared shuttle. The last 18 kilometers before Lanquín are on a badly rutted dirt track—hold on tight. The village of Lanquín itself is a quiet Q'eqchi' settlement with a lovely colonial church and hills covered with coffee plants and cardamom.

The Lanquín Caves open right at the edge of the village—you can walk there from the center. The Cahabón River rises here and plunges underground for several kilometers before resurfacing in the open air. Inside, impressive stalactites and stalagmites fill a series of chambers inhabited by bats. The marked path is roughly 500 to 700 m long. Ideal for getting used to the conditions before the more challenging caves the following day.

Semuc Champey, about 11 km south of Lanquín and about a 45-minute pickup truck ride along a dirt track, is what happens when the Cahabón River—a 196 km watercourse—literally disappears beneath an immense limestone slab 300 meters long. Above it, a series of tiered natural pools have formed, their water shifting from turquoise to emerald green depending on the light and depth. The name comes from Q'eqchi', a local Maya language, and means “where water hides in the stone”. The site is sacred to the surrounding Maya communities. Arrive as early as possible—before 9 am if visiting independently—to enjoy the pools before the organized groups arrive.

The Semuc Champey viewpoint is reached after a 20- to 30-minute climb through the jungle from the site entrance. The climb is strenuous—wear proper shoes, not flip-flops. From the top, the bird's-eye view over all the turquoise pools framed by tropical forest is Guatemala's most famous photograph. Head straight back down to the pools for a swim—the water is cool but very pleasant, especially after the effort.

The K'anba Caves (Cueva de K'anba), near Semuc Champey, offer the most challenging experience on the itinerary: you enter in your swimsuit, candle in hand. The visit involves 20% swimming and 80% wading, with sections where you climb using ropes, natural stone slides and waterfalls to cross. At one point, the guide extinguishes his own lamp so you're left in absolute darkness with nothing but your candle—a striking experience. Let the guide know if you're claustrophobic.

activities.text: Flores-to-Lanquín shared shuttle: a full day on the road that seasoned travelers consider a journey in itself. The climb into the Alta Verapaz mountains, the hair-raising switchbacks and the panoramas over the jungle make it a ride you won't forget. Plan to leave early in the morning from Flores to arrive before dark.

Arrive in Lanquín in the evening and settle into one of the accommodations on the banks of the Cahabón. Most places offer hammocks and riverside terraces—enjoy a quiet dinner after the long day on the road. Look into your next-day excursion to Semuc Champey tonight (all accommodations arrange departures).

River tubing on the Cahabón: seated in a car-tire inner tube, you float downstream for between 30 minutes and 2 hours depending on the water level. Locals sometimes offer refreshing drinks along the banks. It's the ideal late-afternoon activity after Semuc Champey and the caves, to round off a day of adventure.

Swimming at your leisure in the natural pools of Semuc Champey: each pool has its own depth and color. Groups tend to cluster around the first few pools—if you continue a little farther down, you'll find small waterfalls cascading over the limestone, often with barely anyone around. The site has over 100 bird species and 34 mammal species in its immediate surroundings.

visits.text: Livingston can only be reached by boat — no road connects this town to the rest of Guatemala. The lancha from Río Dulce takes about 1h15, heading downriver before rounding the coast to the Caribbean side. Arriving by water, facing this village perched on a limestone bluff, is an unforgettable moment. On land, you won't find Maya markets or embroidered traditional dress: here it's reggaeton and dreadlocks. Livingston is the country's main Garifuna heartland. This people emerged from the intermarriage of shipwrecked Africans (a Nigerian vessel ran aground off Saint Vincent in 1635) and indigenous Caribs, and were later deported by the British to Roatán (Honduras) before gradually migrating to Guatemala in the early 19th century.

Wander through the streets of Livingston to take in the cultural contrast. Garifuna murals on the walls, the scent of coconut in the air, and the beat of primero and segunda drums are a world away from the rest of Guatemala. Be sure to order a tapado, the local signature dish: a stew of shrimp, crab, and fish simmered in spiced coconut milk — the same dish locals have been serving arriving travellers here for the past two centuries.

Follow the coastal trail to the Siete Altares, a series of seven waterfalls and natural pools carved by a creek tumbling downhill to the sea. Allow about 40 minutes on foot from the town centre. The last pool is swimmable and surrounded by dense tropical vegetation. Go in the morning — in the afternoon, the water can rise quickly after upstream rainfall.

activities.text: Catch a live Garifuna music session at one of the waterfront bars in the evening. Punta music, with its drums and polyphonic singing, was originally played at funerals — today it's the soundtrack to every celebration along the Caribbean coast of Central America. The Feast of San Isidro Labrador on May 15 is the town's main annual event.

Take a lancha out to Playa Blanca, a white-sand beach accessible only by boat from Livingston, about twenty minutes away. It's one of the few beaches on Guatemala's Caribbean coast with genuine white sand and translucent water. Local operators arrange full-day trips.

places.name: Melchor De Mencos

visits.text: Melchor de Mencos is the only major road crossing between Guatemala and Belize, set on the Mopán River opposite Benque Viejo del Carmen. The bridge is called Puente de la Amistad, the Bridge of Friendship, despite a territorial dispute never quite fully resolved between the two countries. The crossing operates from 6am to 10pm.

activities.text: Two successive checks await you, Guatemalan exit then Belizean entry, passport in hand for each. Allow twenty minutes to an hour depending on how busy it is. Ignore the informal money changers who approach vehicles: the rate is poor and the service unnecessary, cards are accepted everywhere in Belize.

places.name: Panajachel

visits.text: Lake Atitlán formed roughly 84,000 years ago when a volcanic explosion carved out a caldera several kilometres wide. Today, at 335 metres deep, it is the deepest lake in Central America. Three volcanoes tower over its shores: San Pedro (3,020 m), Tolimán (3,158 m), and Atitlán (3,537 m). Panajachel is the main gateway — Calle Santander, a pedestrianised street lined with handicraft shops, leads straight to the dock. Don't worry if Panajachel feels overly touristy: it's a launchpad, not a destination in itself.

Santa Cruz La Laguna is reachable by lancha from Panajachel (15 minutes) and offers one of the lake's most peaceful panoramas — a small village clinging to a cliff, accessible only by water or via a steep trail from above. No paved road, no cars: just stone houses, lake-facing terraces, and dense vegetation. It's the favourite village of those who want to see the lake without the crowds. Allow an hour and a half on site.

Santiago Atitlán is the capital of the Tz'utujil Maya — the lake's largest indigenous community, whose history stretches back to 900 BC. Take the lancha from Panajachel (25 minutes). As soon as you step off the dock, children will offer to guide you to Maximón: accept — it's the best way to find him. Maximón (also known as San Simón) is a syncretic Maya-Catholic deity whose coral-wood effigy, about one metre tall, is dressed in costumes and 36 neckties. The figure is moved each year to a new family's home — a tremendous honour for the household that receives it. Devotees offer alcohol and cigarettes in exchange for protection. The scene is strange, vivid, and entirely authentic.

The Iglesia Parroquial Santiago Apóstol, built by the Franciscans in 1541, is one of Guatemala's oldest churches. On the entrance walls, plaques commemorate the 'Martyrs of Santiago', including Father Stanley Rother, an American missionary assassinated by paramilitaries in 1981 — his heart was buried here at the request of the Tz'utujil community. Inside, statues of saints are dressed each year by village women in handwoven traditional garments.

San Juan La Laguna, a 15-minute lancha ride from Santiago, is the lake's artisan village: its narrow streets are covered in murals depicting Tz'utujil cosmology, and several women's cooperatives keep alive the tradition of backstrap-loom weaving with natural dyes (the red colour comes from crushed cochineal insects). Step into one of the workshops for a live demonstration — it's free or nearly so.

activities.text: Pre-dawn wake-up for the Indian Nose (Rostro Maya / Nariz del Indio) — this is the defining experience of Lake Atitlán. The 2,093-metre summit above San Juan La Laguna offers a 360° view of the lake and its volcanoes at sunrise. Two options: hike up from San Juan (about 2h30, 492 m of elevation gain) or take a shuttle from Panajachel or San Pedro to Santa Clara (only 30 minutes of climbing, but steeper). Leave at 4 AM to reach the top for golden hour. Going with a guide or local agency is strongly recommended — the trail crosses private land and solo hikers have reported safety issues on certain stretches at night.

Return to the lake in the morning by lancha shuttle from the Panajachel dock to San Pedro La Laguna or San Juan La Laguna. These small collective boats run regularly, connecting villages in 20 to 30 minutes depending on the destination. A lazy afternoon by the water is a welcome reward after the early rise — kayaks and stand-up paddleboards are available for rent in most villages.

In San Juan La Laguna, an artisanal chocolate workshop lets you follow the entire process: from cacao pod to finished bar. Cacao cultivation in the region is an ancestral practice among the Tz'utujil Maya. Allow 30 to 45 minutes for the tour and tasting.

Melipona bees — the stingless bees sacred to the Maya — are kept in a handful of gardens in San Juan. Local operators offer visits to the apiary and tastings of various organic honeys. An unexpected curiosity, and a way to directly support community families.

Head back to Panajachel by lancha in the late afternoon. Catch the sunset from the dock or from one of the rooftop terraces on Calle Santander — the volcanoes silhouetted against the last orange glow in the sky.

places.name: Rio Dulce

visits.text: Catch a bus from Guatemala City heading towards Río Dulce — expect roughly 4 to 5 hours on the road northeast. Along the way, the landscape gradually shifts from the capital's urban sprawl to lush tropical lowlands. Río Dulce is technically the town of Fronteras, nestled on the banks of the river that connects Lake Izabal to the Caribbean Sea. The suspension bridge spanning the río is one of the longest in Central America.

The Castillo de San Felipe de Lara deserves half a day on its own. Built in 1651 by the Spanish at the mouth of Lake Izabal to block English pirates sailing upriver, it was stormed and occupied in 1686, then rebuilt in 1956. Inside you'll find small vaulted rooms, period cannons, and ramparts with unobstructed views over the lake. The site is open daily from 8 AM to 5 PM. If you can, circle it by lancha — the view from the water is even better than from land.

Río Dulce National Park has protected this river corridor since 1955. From the dock at Fronteras, board a lancha and head upstream through the gorge: limestone cliffs rise over 100 metres on either side, draped in vegetation so thick it nearly touches the water's surface. Keep your eyes peeled — grey herons, pelicans, and kingfishers nest in the rock face. Manatees are regular visitors to these calm waters, though spotting one is largely a matter of luck.

Rise before dawn and take a lancha to the Bocas del Polochic Reserve at the western end of Lake Izabal. This 20,760-hectare wetland, designated a Ramsar site in 1996, is formed by the Río Polochic delta. It's Guatemala's main manatee sanctuary — 17th-century Spanish explorers famously mistook them for mermaids. The reserve is also home to 250 bird species (both migratory and resident), river otters, howler monkeys, and, in theory, all five of the country's wild cat species. Leave early: manatees are most likely to surface in the first hours of the morning.

On the way back to Río Dulce along the lake's northern shore, stop at Cañón El Boquerón. This narrow limestone canyon is navigated by rowboat — local guides will drop you off at the entrance. The water is clear, the walls rise about ten metres and are covered in orchids and moss. If you continue on foot through the current, you'll reach a small interior beach. The atmosphere feels almost otherworldly.

activities.text: Paddle through the mangroves on the outskirts of town by kayak or canoe. Local operators rent them out for half-day trips. The atmosphere here is completely different from the main river channel — stilt houses disappear into the vegetation, and fishing dugouts cross your path.

In the late afternoon, head to the hot waterfall at Finca El Paraíso, about twenty kilometres along the northern shore of the lake. A 12-metre cascade of hot water (between 30 and 40°C) plunges into a cold river pool — the contrast feels like a natural jungle spa. The spot is popular with locals on weekends, so try to go on a weekday if you can.

Birdwatching at sunrise on Lake Izabal — the 50 km-long, 20 km-wide lake sees few visitors, and the conditions for birdlife are exceptional. Keel-billed toucans, cormorants, and egrets share the waters. Bring binoculars.

Evening swim in the river from the dock of your lodge. Río Dulce is home to several eco-lodges on stilts built directly over the water — some have no road access at all and can only be reached by boat, which gives the whole experience a timeless, off-the-grid feel.

visits.text: Sacapulas sits in an arid canyon at just 1,200 metres, even though the road descends to it from passes above 3,000. The climatic contrast is stark after just an hour's descent. The bridge over the Río Negro and the small-scale salt pans on its banks are the only two things worth seeing: it is a technical stop, not a cultural stage.

activities.text: Break the Huehuetenango-Cobán route here, rather than facing seven to eight hours of mountain driving in one go. The comedores in the town serve a decent lunch around the square, and it is the last reliable place to stock up before Uspantán. Fill up with fuel, as petrol stations become scarce afterwards.

places.name: San Juan Comalapa

visits.text: A cemetery wall as an art gallery: in San Juan Comalapa, the mural running along the Cementerio General tells the country's history, from pre-Columbian times to the armed conflict. The village's painters undertook it collectively from the 1990s onwards. Park below and walk up, as it reads in that direction.

Comalapa's painting tradition began in the 1930s with Andrés Curruchich (1891-1969), who took up oil painting to depict scenes of Kaqchikel life. His pupils carried the style on, hence the nickname "Florencia de América". The childhood home of Rafael Álvarez Ovalle, composer of the national anthem, can also be visited in the town.

activities.text: Painters' workshops often occupy the artists' own houses, around the square, and the door opens without ceremony. You buy directly from the creator, and the canvases are rolled up for transport. The village's craft market is more modest than Chichicastenango's, but considerably less crowded.

places.name: San Juan La Laguna

visits.text: Calle de las Sombrillas climbs from the San Juan La Laguna jetty towards the centre, beneath a ceiling of colourful umbrellas. The façades on both sides are painted by village artists on Mayan themes. It is short, a five-minute walk, but it is the backbone of the town: everything starts from there.

San Juan's painting galleries are worth more than their reputation as tourist shops suggests. The local naive style depicts daily life and Mayan legends, often seen from above, as if the painter were perched overhead. Sellers roll up the canvases for transport, which solves the luggage question.

activities.text: You will visit one of the Tz'utujil weavers' cooperatives, where the cotton is dyed using only plants: indigo, avocado bark, cochineal. The backstrap loom demonstration lasts around twenty minutes and needs no appointment. Some cooperatives also offer workshops lasting several hours, to be booked the day before.

A village café worth the detour: the La Voz cooperative brings together producer families from the surrounding plots and gives tours of its plantations. The tour covers varieties, altitude and processing, then finishes with a cup. The café next door, on the main street, serves the same beans if time is short.

visits.text: Santiago Atitlán was the capital of the Tz'utujil kingdom before the Spanish conquest, and most inhabitants still speak Tz'utujil among themselves. The colonial church, on the square, dates back to the 16th century and retains period altarpieces and statues. A plaque there recalls the murder of the American priest Stanley Rother in 1981, during the armed conflict.

Here he is not called Maximón but Rilaj Mam, "the Great Grandfather". This dressed wooden figure, wearing a hat and smoking a cigar, moves house each year according to the ritual calendar: the boatmen and guides at the jetty know where to find him. A modest offering is expected, a second one if you take photographs.

Stacks of textiles, medicinal herbs, live poultry: Santiago Atitlán's market operates first and foremost for people from the neighbouring villages. Huipiles embroidered on a backstrap loom, with their bird motifs, are distinctive to Tz'utujil women. Tuesdays and Fridays are the busiest days; the rest of the week, things quieten down.

activities.text: You will cross the lake by private boat from Panajachel, around forty minutes depending on the state of the water. The crossing gives the best angle on the three volcanoes, better than any viewpoint on land. Sit at the front on the way out, at the back on the way back when the Xocomil picks up.

visits.text: Sayaxché is crossed by ferry: no bridge spans the Río La Pasión here, vehicles board a cable barge. The town serves as a base for around ten Mayan sites in the area, Ceibal and Aguateca chief among them. Expect a wait at the ferry in mid-morning, when lorries pile up.

activities.text: The last real supply point before the Cráter Azul: petrol, ice, water and provisions are found here, not beyond. Lancha operators also have offices in town, which remains the best place to lock in the boat price before reaching the jetty.

days_plan.itin_title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean

visits.text: Semuc Champey comes down to a single geological anomaly: the Río Cahabón disappears beneath a natural limestone bridge 300 metres long, and above it tiered turquoise pools are fed by springs. The Q'eqchi' name means 'where the river hides under the stone'. A natural monument since 2005; entry around 50 quetzales.

The mirador is the only spot from which Semuc Champey makes sense, and it has to be earned: 45 minutes of steep climbing through the jungle, steps and roots. Do it first, before the heat and before swimming. Coming back down drenched in sweat, the pools take on their full meaning.

activities.text: You'll swim in the tiered pools, the deepest of which reaches about three metres. The travertine is slippery underwater: walk rather than jump and watch for the ledges between pools. Arrive before 10am or after 2.30pm to avoid the crowds and enjoy low-angled light.

A rustic but perfectly guided adventure: the K'an Ba cave is explored candle in hand, waist-deep in water in places. Narrow passages, small waterfalls, slippery rocks. Tubing on the Cahabón is available right next door. Neither is included in your quote: pay on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean

visits.text: Temple IV rises 65 meters, Tikal's tallest pyramid (La Danta at El Mirador, even taller, demands five days of jungle trekking to reach). Built around 741 under the reign of Yik'in Chan K'awiil, it marked the western boundary of the ceremonial center. The wooden staircase leads to the summit where the canopy opens endlessly, pierced by other temple peaks. Sunrise bookings possible, 5:30am on site, sometimes foggy conditions.

Howler monkeys wake Tikal's jungle before dawn—their deep roar carries for several kilometers. The national park covers 576 km² and shelters jaguars, coatis, toucans, over 400 bird species. You'll walk fifteen kilometers in the day—bring water and closed-toe shoes.

Tikal's Gran Plaza aligns two pyramids face to face: Temple I (45 meters, Temple of the Great Jaguar, 682-734) and Temple II (38 meters). The North Acropolis and Central Acropolis border them—you can climb the latter for plunging views. The nobles' residential palace contains about a hundred rooms.

El Mundo Perdido is worth the detour—Tikal's oldest complex, built in the Preclassic era and abandoned around 900 AD. The ceremonial pyramid rises 30 meters—you can climb it for 360° views far less crowded than the Gran Plaza.

Local guides say that George Lucas filmed the rebel base scene on Yavin 4 here for Star Wars Episode IV in 1977. The city peaked between 600 and 800, with up to 60,000 inhabitants in the heart of the urban area.

activities.text: If you can handle a 4am wake-up, the 'sunrise' tour leaves before official opening and places visitors atop Temple IV for sunrise. Mist, howlers, first light on the pyramids—it's the trip's most memorable experience. Count on 250 to 350 quetzals with guide.

Spot coatis, keel-billed toucans, and spider monkeys on trails between temple groups. Morning and late afternoon are best. A naturalist guide makes all the difference—otherwise you'll miss half the animals.

visits.text: Dormant for nearly a century, the Pacaya volcano woke violently in 1965 and has barely stopped being active since. Its active crater bears the name of Alfredo MacKenney, a Guatemalan doctor who monitored its evolution for decades. The park is open from 7am to 6pm: leave Antigua early, as clouds often roll in after 11am and blot out the view.

activities.text: You will climb Pacaya with a local guide: this is the park's rule, and useful anyway for reading the landscape. Allow about 3 hours there and back over 5km, with modest elevation gain. Horses wait at the trailhead for those who would rather spare their legs, for an extra fee negotiated on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Guatemala and Belize in 15 Days: Mayan Cities and the Caribbean

visits.text: Yaxha has neither Tikal's size nor its crowds, and that's exactly what makes it worthwhile. One of Petén's major sites, it counts about 500 structures including 9 temple-pyramids, all on the lagoon's edge. Do it before Tikal so you won't be disappointed, or do it for the sunset.

Temple 216 rises 37 meters above the canopy and offers the signature view: Yaxha lagoon, the Topoxté site on its islet, and jungle stretching to the horizon. The wooden staircase replaces the stone stairway that became impassable. Yaxha means 'green water' in Maya, a name unchanged since the Classic era.

Iguanas dart through the stones and howler monkeys settle in trees above the stelae. The minor astronomical complex, erected between 700 and 800 AD, aligns stelae and a four-step pyramid with the solstices. Stela 31 and its carved birds on Plaza F.

activities.text: Stay until sunset atop Temple 216—it's the site's signature experience. Silence is broken only by howlers and toucans returning for the night. Bring water, headlamp for the descent, and strong repellent: mosquitoes emerge at 5pm.
